newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German building sector starts '97 wage round.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German building sector starts '97 wage round.

text.p: Germany's construction sector entered its 1997 wage round on Tuesday with trade union IG Bau announcing that it would seek to ensure that wages for the 1.3 million workers in the industry did not fall in real terms.

But union officials said they would not name the precise level of the wage rise they would accept because it was only one part of a package of demands they would put to employers in an industry still struggling with its labour relations.
"We shall not be naming any figure in any form yet," IG Bau chairman Klaus Wiesehuegel told a news briefing.

Wiesehuegel said however the union saw other wage accords, such as those reached in the large metal and engineering sectors, as "guiding indicators". German inflation is widely expected to remain around 1.5 percent during 1997.

Agreements based around wage rises of 1.5 percent and 2.5 percent in 1997 and 1998 have been struck for the vast majority of Germany's 3.2 million metal and engineering workers, deals widely seen as moderate.

IG Bau will enter negotiations with employers late next month with a package of demands including the reinstatement of a 13th-month end-of-year bonus and of sick pay entitlements at 100 percent of salary.

It also wants clear agreements on payment of compensation to workers during bad weather, which this winter is expected to have helped push unemployment in the sector to some 400,000 -- a third of all German construction workers.

Last year building workers were awarded a 1.85 percent pay increase, but controversy in the industry has remained over the continued disparity between west and east German wages and use of low-paid foreign workers.

A spokesman for the construction employer federation ZDB said it would be looking at the details of wage demand before making a reaction but noted that the issue of sick pay entitlements, which have recently been cut, was not negotiable.
"Existing clauses on sick pay run until the end of the year," a ZDB spokesman said, confirming that wage negotiations are due to start in Frankfurt on February 27.

Sick pay in the sector was cut to 80 percent following a federal law introduced in October last year. Huge resistance by metal and engineering workers meant the law was not implemented in new wage contracts for those industries.
The new wage round comes after the generally-binding minimum wage deal agreed for construction workers last November and due to run as a trial till August 31 this year.
The accord sets west German wages at 17 marks and east German wages at 15.64 marks an hour -- some way down on the 18.60 and 17.11 marks respectively that IG Bau had orginally sought.

Construction analysts said that large contractors, which are already suffering from fierce price pressure, slow economic growth and a lack of building investment, would be little affected by a wage rise in the sector around or slightly above inflation.

"There is an increasing use by the large firms of subcontractors (which will absorb much of the pay rise). It will be on the smaller and medium firms that most of the impact will be seen," one analyst said.
